meter.definition: The base unit of length in the International System of Units (SI). Defined as the length of the path traveled by light in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second.
meter.history: Originally defined in 1793 as one ten-millionth of the distance from the equator to the North Pole.
meter.used_for: Measuring distances, room dimensions, height, and scientific lengths.
examples: Height of a standard doorway (~2 meters)
Length of an Olympic swimming pool (50 meters)

kilometer.definition: A unit of length equal to 1,000 meters.
kilometer.history: Introduced during the French Revolution as part of the metric system adoption.
kilometer.used_for: Road distances, geographical measurements, and athletic races.
examples: A typical 5K running race (5 km)
Distance between city centers

centimeter.definition: A unit of length equal to 1/100th of a meter.
centimeter.history: Part of the centimetre-gram-second (CGS) system of units.
centimeter.used_for: Body measurements, clothing dimensions, and small objects.
examples: Width of a standard credit card (~8.5 cm)
Diameter of a US penny (~1.9 cm)

inch.definition: A unit of length equal to 2.54 centimeters in the imperial and US customary systems.
inch.history: Historically defined as the width of a human thumb, later standardized to 3 barleycorns.
inch.used_for: Screen sizes, display dimensions, rain measurement, and carpentry.
examples: Smartphone screen size (e.g. 6.1 inches)
Standard paper width (8.5 inches)

foot.definition: A unit of length equal to 12 inches or 0.3048 meters.
foot.history: Based on the average human foot length; standardized internationally in 1959.
foot.used_for: Aviation altitudes, human height in US/UK, and building construction.
examples: Cruising altitude of a commercial airliner (~35,000 feet)
Average height of an adult male (~5 feet 9 inches)

mile.definition: A unit of distance equal to 5,280 feet or 1,609.344 meters.
mile.history: Derived from the Roman 'mille passus', meaning one thousand double-steps.
mile.used_for: Highway speed limits and long-distance travel in US and UK.
examples: Full marathon distance (26.2 miles)
Distance traveled at 60 mph in one hour

kilogram.definition: The SI base unit of mass. Defined by fixing the numerical value of Planck's constant (h) to 6.62607015×10⁻³⁴ J·s.
kilogram.history: Redefined in 2019 away from the physical International Prototype Kilogram (IPK) cylinder.
kilogram.used_for: Body weight, grocery items, cargo, and scientific mass measurements.
examples: A standard bag of flour or sugar (1 kg)
Average weight of a newborn human (~3.5 kg)

gram.definition: A unit of mass equal to 1/1,000th of a kilogram.
gram.history: Originally defined in 1795 as the absolute weight of a volume of pure water equal to the cube of the hundredth part of a meter at freezing.
gram.used_for: Nutritional labels, cooking recipes, precious metals, and medication.
examples: Mass of a standard paperclip (~1 gram)
Recommended daily salt intake (~5 grams)

pound.definition: A unit of mass equal to 16 ounces or exactly 0.45359237 kilograms.
pound.history: From the Latin 'libra pondo', meaning weight measured in pounds.
pound.used_for: Body weight in US/UK, produce weight, and shipping packages.
examples: Weight of a loaf of bread (~1 pound)
Standard bowling ball weight (10 to 16 lbs)

ounce.definition: A unit of mass equal to 1/16th of a pound or ~28.3495 grams.
ounce.history: Derived from the Latin 'uncia', meaning a twelfth part.
ounce.used_for: Food portioning, mail weights, and small package shipping.
examples: A single slice of cheese (~1 ounce)
Standard letter weight limit for basic postage (1 oz)

celsius.definition: A temperature scale where 0 °C is the freezing point of water and 100 °C is the boiling point at standard sea level pressure.
celsius.history: Invented by Swedish astronomer Anders Celsius in 1742.
celsius.used_for: Everyday weather, medical body temperature, and scientific applications outside the US.
examples: Normal human body temperature (37 °C)
Comfortable indoor room temperature (20–22 °C)

fahrenheit.definition: A temperature scale where water freezes at 32 °F and boils at 212 °F under standard atmospheric pressure.
fahrenheit.history: Proposed in 1724 by physicist Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit based on an ice-salt mixture.
fahrenheit.used_for: Weather forecasts, cooking ovens, and thermostat settings in the United States.
examples: Baking temperature for cakes (~350 °F)
Hot summer weather day (90–100 °F)

kelvin.definition: The SI base unit of thermodynamic temperature. Absolute zero is 0 K.
kelvin.history: Named after William Thomson, 1st Baron Kelvin, who wrote of the need for an absolute thermometric scale in 1848.
kelvin.used_for: Physics, astronomy, thermodynamics, and light color temperature.
examples: Freezing point of water (273.15 K)
Warm white LED light bulb color (2700–3000 K)

byte.definition: A unit of digital information consisting of 8 bits.
byte.history: Coined by Werner Buchholz in 1956 during the design of the IBM Stretch computer.
byte.used_for: Character encoding (ASCII/UTF-8), memory addressing, and file size measurements.
examples: A single ASCII text character (1 byte)
Short text message (~100–200 bytes)

gigabyte.definition: A unit of digital data storage equal to 1,000,000,000 bytes (decimal) or 1,073,741,824 bytes (binary/GiB).
gigabyte.history: Became common in personal computing during the late 1990s as hard drives expanded.
gigabyte.used_for: RAM capacity, smartphone storage, video files, and internet data plans.
examples: High-definition movie download (~2–4 GB)
Standard smartphone RAM (6 GB to 12 GB)

liter.definition: A metric unit of volume equal to 1 cubic decimeter (1,000 cubic centimeters).
liter.history: Introduced in France in 1795 as one of the original metric units.
liter.used_for: Beverages, engine displacement, fuel tank capacity, and liquid measurements.
examples: Standard bottled soda size (2 liters)
Automobile fuel tank capacity (45–65 liters)

gallon_us.definition: A US unit of liquid volume equal to 128 US fluid ounces or ~3.7854 liters.
gallon_us.history: Derived from the English wine gallon standard used before 1824.
gallon_us.used_for: Gasoline sales, milk jugs, and paint containers in the United States.
examples: Standard jug of milk in US supermarkets (1 gallon)
Standard paint bucket (1 gallon or 5 gallons)

watt.definition: The SI unit of power, equal to 1 joule per second.
watt.history: Named after James Watt, inventor of the steam engine condenser.
watt.used_for: Light bulb ratings, electrical appliance power consumption, and audio speaker power.
examples: LED light bulb power consumption (9–12 W)
Microwave oven heating power (800–1200 W)

volt.definition: The SI unit of electric potential difference and electromotive force.
volt.history: Named in honor of Alessandro Volta, inventor of the voltaic pile (first chemical battery).
volt.used_for: Battery voltage ratings, household electrical outlets, and electronic circuits.
examples: Standard AA battery voltage (1.5 V)
USB charging port voltage (5 V DC)
